notes: Ordinary U.S. Treasury bill held to maturity, sold at a discount or par. Bank discount rate uses face value and a 360-day year: price = face × (1 − discount × days / 360). This rate is not the return on your purchase cost. All entered rates are assumptions or your quote, not live auction data.

Holding-period gross return = (face − price) / price. Simple annualized gross yield uses your selected 365- or 366-day year and does not compound. It is NOT the official Treasury auction Investment Rate or a promise of a broker bond-equivalent yield, particularly for longer bills with different quotation conventions.

Hypothetical effective annual yield compounds the gross holding-period return assuming repeated reinvestment at the same return for a full selected year. This is a comparison convention, not interest paid each day or a reinvestment forecast. No accrued-balance growth curve is fabricated: the table shows only purchase and maturity cash flows.

Federal tax is a simplified estimate on positive gross discount interest using your federal plus optional additional investment-income tax rate. Bill interest is exempt from state/local income tax. The fee reduces net cash return but is not deducted from the tax base; basis adjustments, AMT, tax-year accrual, withholding and personal NIIT eligibility are not calculated. Tax is shown at maturity for comparison, not as an actual filing/payment schedule.

Face value uses $100 increments. Enter actual settlement-to-maturity days, excluding the settlement day; standard week shortcuts are nominal days, not a dated settlement or holiday calendar. The year-day selector affects annualized returns only, never the 360-day bank-discount price. Secondary sales, price premiums, reinvestment ladders, brokerage-specific charges and tax-advantaged accounts require different analysis. Internal prices retain precision; actual auction/broker rounding can differ.

notes: Regular method for U.S. nonfarm business profit, tax years 2025/2026. Enter net profit after business expenses, not gross revenue or income after personal deductions. Net losses produce zero SE tax here; one spouse’s loss does not reduce the other spouse’s SE earnings. Special farm/nonfarm optional methods, church employees, railroad compensation, foreign agreements and other special cases are excluded.

Regular SE tax uses 92.35% of positive profit, with no regular tax below $400 adjusted earnings. Social Security is 12.4% up to each taxpayer’s remaining 2026 wage base of $184,500; Medicare is 2.9% without that cap. Enter Social Security wages separately from Medicare wages because W-2 boxes 3 and 5 can differ.

The primary result includes regular SE tax plus the SE portion of 0.9% Additional Medicare tax. It excludes ordinary federal income tax, state taxes, wage FICA, and wage-only Additional Medicare. The deductible half excludes Additional Medicare and is an income adjustment, not a dollar-for-dollar tax credit.

Quarterly reserve simply divides the SE result by four. It is not a Form 1040-ES payment, safe-harbor calculation or required installment schedule. Actual estimated payments depend on total tax, prior-year tax, withholding and timing.

covered-call.label: Baseline

focus.label: Covered call profit / loss at your expiry price

metrics.label: Covered call profit / loss at your expiry price
Worst-case loss at zero stock price
Shares-only profit / loss at your expiry price
Expiry return on net initial debit
Maximum expiry return on net initial debit

notes: Standard USD stock buy-write only: purchase exactly 100 shares for every short call contract. Stock entry price is the price used for this new trade, not historical tax basis or an existing holding’s lifetime performance. Adjusted contracts, extra uncovered shares, naked calls, synthetic calls and poor man’s covered calls are not modeled.

At expiry, stock plus short-call economic value = shares × min(stock price, strike). Profit/loss = that value − net initial debit − entered expiry exit costs. Stock value below strike is marked to market rather than automatically sold. The shares-only alternative uses the same stock purchase fee and expiry exit allowance but has neither premium nor option opening fees; unused premium cash is not reinvested.

Premium is entered per share, not per contract. Total premium = premium × 100 × contracts. It is gross cash received, not pure profit: stock losses and trading costs can outweigh it. This tool does not estimate a fair premium, quote a live option chain or recommend a security.

Net initial debit = stock purchase + stock purchase fees + option opening fees − premium. Returns divide expiry P/L by that positive debit, not by strike, gross stock cost or a broker margin requirement. Worst-case loss magnitude includes the entered fixed exit cost even at zero stock value. A negative maximum profit means no modeled expiry price produces a profit.

The break-even price includes entry and exit fees. If it exceeds strike, the capped strategy has no break-even under these assumptions; increasing the expiry stock price cannot fix it. A covered call retains substantial stock downside and caps gains at strike. The price-scenario chart shows outcomes, not probabilities or an expected stock-price path.

The simple annualized maximum return multiplies the one-trade maximum return by 365 / entered calendar days. It is not compounded, a forecast, an APY or guaranteed repeatable income; days do not change the expiry payoff. It assumes no new trades or reinvestment.

Actual assignment can occur before expiry, particularly around dividends, and exercise decisions near strike can vary. This expiry-only model does not predict assignment, ex-dividend dates or proceeds from closing early. Dividends, taxes, interest, financing, bid/ask slippage, volatility, time value before expiry, rolls and broker-specific fees are excluded unless represented in the flat entered cost allowances.

Dividends, taxes, interest, financing, bid/ask slippage, volatility, time value before expiry, rolls and broker-specific fees are excluded unless represented in the flat entered cost allowances.

credit-card-minimum-payment.label: Baseline
notes: This is a user-defined single-balance estimate, not the minimum due on your actual statement. Interest is opening balance × APR / 12. Percentage amount is opening balance × minimum percentage; add monthly interest to that amount only when Yes is selected. Take the larger of this amount and the dollar floor, capped by balance plus interest.

The extra amount is added above each recalculated minimum, not used to hold the total payment fixed. As a percentage minimum declines, the total monthly payment may decline too. The final payment is capped at the amount owed. A dollar floor can repay a small remaining balance sooner.

No new purchases, fees, past-due amounts, grace periods, promotional rate changes, multiple APR balances or installment-plan amounts are modeled. Real card issuers often accrue interest daily, use statement balances and round charges or minimums differently. Refer to your cardmember agreement and current statement for the actual required amount.

Internal calculations retain fractional cents and round only for display. Small differences from statement rounding accumulate over a long schedule. The supported estimate ends within 1,200 months (100 years); non-amortizing or longer paths return an error rather than a payoff promise.

Savings compare the same balance, APR and minimum rule with and without your selected extra payment. If the minimum-only path is not repayable under supported rules, savings are undefined. New borrowing and changes to the minimum formula can invalidate the comparison. No credit-score, lender-approval or affordability assessment is made.
